medical.title: A doctor's guide to surviving—and enjoying—holiday feasting while on GLP‑1 medication
medical.summary: Thanksgiving and the winter holidays bring celebration, connection and plenty of opportunities to come together with family and friends.

medical.title: Experimental anesthetic may also blunt pain at nonsedating doses
medical.summary: Common intravenous anesthetics such as propofol and etomidate usually require additional pain medicines. Propofol and etomidate enhance GABA-A receptors, which act as brakes on nerve-cell activity, but generally do not relieve pain at nonsedating doses. In addition, propofol is known to commonly cause low blood pressure and slowed (or sometimes stopped) breathing, while etomidate can cause adrenal suppression by lowering cortisol production, potentially causing severe or life-threatening effects. Therefore, researchers are looking for suitable alternatives.

medical.title: New cancer frontiers: Could COVID vaccines help make treatments more effective?
medical.summary: Recent years have brought extraordinary advances in vaccines and treatments that harness our immune systems.

medical.title: Some allergies may start with cells running short of energy, not immune system misfires
medical.summary: Scientists are challenging centuries-old teaching that allergies start in the immune system, suggesting instead that they may be due to a power failure inside the body's barrier cells, which line the skin, gut, nose, lungs and esophagus.

medical.title: Could an erectile dysfunction drug offer a new way to treat Alzheimer's?
medical.summary: A drug developed to treat erectile dysfunction might seem an unlikely treatment for Alzheimer's disease. But researchers are increasingly interested in whether medicines such as Viagra could also help protect the brain.

medical.title: Resistance training could help boost brain health and confidence in older adults
medical.summary: Think about the last time you stood up from a chair or lifted a heavy shopping bag from the floor. These movements might feel automatic, but they take a surprising amount of coordination between your brain and your muscles.

medical.title: Genetic data from over one million people reveals new clues to how endometriosis develops
medical.summary: In a large, international study analyzing data from over 1 million people, researchers identified multiple genomic regions, associations and pathways underlying endometriosis, a debilitating, chronic condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows in other places in the body.

medical.title: Opioid misuse recognized, but not always recorded, national survey finds
medical.summary: Primary care clinicians who recognized opioid misuse in their patients did not always record it in the medical record, according to a national survey of 1,470 clinicians led by researchers at Wake Forest University School of Medicine.

medical.title: PTSD may shape the human brain differently depending on gender, race and the age at which a person's trauma occurred
medical.summary: Stress and trauma can leave molecular marks in the brain that may help explain the development of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). A study published in the journal Cell Reports on Nov. 20 that examined the postmortem brains of 101 people with PTSD found that genes associated with PTSD varied more than expected across different brain regions when it comes to DNA methylation, a natural biological process that acts like a genetic "dimmer switch" for genes, sometimes blocking genetic code entirely.

medical.title: Late-night phone use linked to shorter sleep in teens, especially girls
medical.summary: Checking the first notification after turning off the wake-up alarm, then endlessly scrolling through reels until sleepy. For many teenagers, the phone is never too far away. Excessive screen time has been linked to physical and mental health problems among teenagers, and its tentacles run deeper for the age group that is particularly vulnerable to body image issues. Scientists suspect the effects can extend beyond waking hours, reaching into an essential part of the body's daily routine: sleep.

medical.title: New liver model for studying alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency
medical.summary: AATD is a rare genetic metabolic disorder that affects the liver and lungs. A mutation causes liver cells (hepatocytes) to form misfolded alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT). This misfolding results in reduced secretion of AAT into the blood plasma. AAT plays an important role in controlling inflammatory processes in the body by mitigating excessive reactions that lead to tissue damage.

medical.title: MYC inhibitor drug targets cancer cells directly and via the immune system
medical.summary: In a series of experiments, researchers have found that an experimental MYC inhibitor drug not only targets lung cancer cells directly but also makes cancer cells easier for the immune system to target and kill.

medical.title: High blood sugar powers an experimental implant that helps improve glucose control in diabetes
medical.summary: High blood sugar, a major problem in type 2 diabetes, could become part of the solution in monitoring the disease. Researchers have developed an experimental implant called NeuroAxis that utilizes a glucose fuel cell to harvest energy and sense metabolic fluctuations in real time.

medical.title: A protein in the brain's immune cells may accelerate damage in Alzheimer's disease
medical.summary: Researchers at Lund University in Sweden have identified a key role for the protein galectin-3 in Alzheimer's disease. The study shows that galectin-3 not only influences how the brain's immune cells, known as microglia, react to the disease's characteristic amyloid plaques but also shapes the plaques themselves—and may contribute to the nerve damage that develops around them.

medical.title: Malaria antibody protects infants but lowers immune response to R21 vaccine, trial finds
medical.summary: A single intramuscular dose of an experimental malaria monoclonal antibody safely provided infants with strong protection during Mali's six-month malaria season. However, potential interference with the R21 malaria vaccine is putting plans to pursue development of L9LS for this age group on hold, according to results from a clinical trial presented at the annual meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (ASTMH).

medical.title: Malaria vaccine shows 87% efficacy in clinical trial
medical.summary: The novel, genetically attenuated whole-parasite PfSPZ-LARC2 Vaccine for malaria achieved an 87% efficacy rate in preventing infection during a recent phase 1 trial.

medical.title: Gut stem cells go into overdrive with age—now scientists see a way to restrain their growth
medical.summary: A telltale sign of shortened life expectancy emerges in the gut with a hyperproliferation of stem cells, report scientists who have documented a dysregulation of these cells and defined them as a marker for aging across several species.

medical.title: Public code is not always reusable: Review uncovers gaps in medical study documentation
medical.summary: The data and code that underpin a research study can tell us what was actually done, and how. In a medical study, for example, how were patients selected for inclusion? How were missing values handled? How were the results evaluated? Access to a study's data and code helps researchers to answer these questions, to examine the methods and to build on the work.

medical.title: World-first study identifies genetic markers of young-onset type 2 diabetes in Chinese population
medical.summary: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK)'s Faculty of Medicine (CU Medicine) has conducted the world's first and largest genetic association study of age at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes in a Chinese population. The study identified three genetic regions associated with younger disease onset, impaired insulin-producing beta-cell function, and poorer blood glucose control.

medical.title: National study highlights flexible approaches to integrating pharmacists in aged care
medical.summary: A national study led by researchers from RMIT University and the University of Canberra (UC) has identified practical strategies to support the integration of on-site pharmacists in residential elder care homes across metropolitan, regional, rural and remote Australia.

medical.title: Insecticide exposure in pregnancy linked to cognition in middle childhood
medical.summary: Neonicotinoids are among the most common insecticides worldwide, given their low cost and high efficacy. However, these insecticides take a long time to break down in the environment and can easily contaminate their surroundings, affecting food and water supplies. Despite the well-documented effects of neonicotinoids on insects and the environment, their impact on humans remains less clear.

medical.title: What is 'fascia release' and do I need to do it? A physical therapy expert unpacks the evidence
medical.summary: Are your hips constantly "tight"? Do you have bad posture? Are you stressed? According to the wellness world, it's probably your fascia (pronounced "FASH-ah"). This is the new buzzword explanation for many of your ailments: your fascia is tight, stuck, stiff or even dehydrated—and you need to "release" it.

medical.title: Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months
medical.summary: A new clinical trial found that the ketogenic diet dramatically outperformed Mediterranean and low-fat diets in reducing liver fat and improving metabolic health, even when participants lost similar amounts of weight. After just four to five months, about half of those following keto no longer met the criteria for prediabetes, while their liver fat dropped by an average of 67%.

medical.title: Molecular glues: Unlocking new targets in cancer
medical.summary: The human genome encodes several hundred E3 ligases—the enzymes that decide which proteins a cell destroys. Drug developers have so far harnessed a small number of them. In a new review in Molecular Cell, researchers at Karolinska Institutet and the University of Verona argue that the rest of these E3 ligases are where the next generation of cancer drugs will be found.

medical.title: This simple habit is linked to a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's
medical.summary: Reading for pleasure may have surprisingly powerful benefits for the brain, with studies linking it to better memory, reduced stress, improved mental health, and a lower risk of dementia. Researchers highlight findings that just five minutes of fiction can reduce stress by up to 20%, while reading has also been associated with a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.

science.title: Spiders, beetles and one garage alligator: Largest study to date reveals wildlife sharing our indoor spaces
science.summary: An international team of researchers is revealing the largest study to date detailing the wide range of insects, arachnids and other organisms that live in homes and other indoor environments across the United States and Canada. The researchers have compiled a database with more than 20,000 entries spanning more than 2,000 species found in these indoor ecosystems.

science.title: Deep Venture: A new class of ocean exploration vehicle developed
science.summary: Researchers have a new capability for exploring some of the least understood regions of the ocean. Developed by Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) in collaboration with NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, Deep Venture is a next-generation autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) for deep-ocean research, capable of supporting a wide range of scientific missions, from shallow coastal waters to the deepest places on Earth. It can withstand extreme pressure, rated for depths of up to 11,000 meters (about 6.83 mi), or full ocean depth.

science.title: Anthropic researcher says Claude solved math's greatest riddle
science.summary: A mathematician at AI company Anthropic said Friday that he had used the firm's Claude chatbot to prove the Riemann hypothesis, a problem that has eluded mathematicians for more than 160 years.

science.title: A new way to extract oxygen from lunar soil could support bases on the moon
science.summary: Computer chip manufacturing and lunar exploration seem like completely different worlds. Yet our latest research suggests the two may be more closely connected than expected.

science.title: Theory explains how fusion plasmas enter a state of improved energy confinement, solving a 40-year puzzle
science.summary: Nuclear fusion promises a source of energy by combining light atomic nuclei, the same process that powers the sun. To achieve fusion on Earth, scientists must heat a gas to extreme temperatures, creating a charged state of matter called plasma. Keeping this plasma hot and stable long enough for fusion energy production is one of the main challenges facing the technology.

science.title: More worried, yet more hopeful: The paradox of young people's climate action
science.summary: New research from NIHR School of Public Health Research, published in the Lancet Planetary Health, provides new insights into how taking action on climate can impact young people's climate change distress, mental health and well-being.

science.title: Killer whales became fearsome predators long before scientists thought
science.summary: Killer whales, or orcas, are among the ocean's most formidable predators, hunting everything from fish and seals to other whales. But how and when these members of the dolphin family evolved into such effective hunters has long been something of a mystery.

science.title: How desert biocrusts respond to changing snow cover
science.summary: In the desert, winter snow may seem like a temporary visitor, but its effects can last long after the snow melts. By supplying water to dry ecosystems, snowfall helps sustain biological soil crusts (biocrusts), thin living layers on the soil surface that play important roles in desert ecosystems.

science.title: Excitons mimic light in atom-thin material, confirming decade-old quantum prediction
science.summary: Combining their skills in theory and experiment, Yale researchers have observed for the first time a type of energy-carrying composite particle move in a highly unexpected way. It's a finding that could lead to advances in quantum technologies, solar energy, LEDs and other optoelectronic technologies. The work is published in Nature Physics.

science.title: Researchers trace shifting pulsation modes in δ Scuti star KIC 4737720
science.summary: Stars in the night sky may look calm and unchanging, but some are in fact constantly "vibrating." Just as a musical instrument can sound several notes at once, a star can pulse in several modes simultaneously. By measuring minute changes in a star's brightness, astronomers can read these stellar vibrations and, in turn, probe the physical processes at work inside it.

science.title: Venus-like conditions reveal how minerals could preserve traces of ancient water
science.summary: Venus is one of the most inhospitable environments in our solar system, with surface temperatures hot enough to melt lead and atmospheric pressure nearly 100 times greater than Earth's. Yet its surface may preserve clues to a time when the planet looked much more like Earth.

science.title: Male bumblebees contribute to nest care, challenging view that they only mate
science.summary: For decades, researchers have assumed male bumblebees' contribution to hives consisted mainly of DNA. However, a new study finds that the males actually help incubate baby bumbles, and that with males' assistance, hives thrive. The study, published in the Royal Society Open Science journal, quantifies the beneficial effects of having male babysitters in the hive.

science.title: Low-viscosity lavas reveal a key to Mars's past
science.summary: Since 2021, the Mars Perseverance rover has been roaming Jezero Crater, gathering details about the red planet's geology and hints about its past. On its journey, the rover took close-up images of the Séítah formation, a nearly 4-billion-year-old layer of rock at the base of the crater.

science.title: Mobile streaming habits offer global societal insights
science.summary: Researchers from the University of the Sunshine Coast observed how a total of 959 consumers in the U.S., South Korea and Germany used mobile streaming services.

science.title: A star's last gasps: ALMA reveals a giant gas ring and budding hourglass around a star in transition
science.summary: Stars like our sun don't die quietly. In their final act, they swell into red giants, shed their outer layers into space and leave behind a glowing, often strikingly sculpted cloud of gas called a planetary nebula. That transformation is thought to take only a few thousand years, a blink in the life of a star, so catching one in the act is rare.

science.title: We found a seaweed that hadn't been spotted in 90 years—and discovered vast underwater forests
science.summary: A tangle of long, caramel-colored seaweed. That's what botanist A.H.S. Lucas found in 1935 while conducting research near Lord Howe Island, a World Heritage–listed site known for its unique biodiversity. After collecting some large adult specimens of this previously unidentified seaweed, Lucas named it Sargassum howeanum.

science.title: New model predicts critical temperature of superconductors
science.summary: Superconductivity, the ability to carry current with no resistance, has been found in materials ranging from metals to oxides. Conventional Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) theory explains low-temperature metal superconductors well, but struggles with high-temperature oxide superconductors.

science.title: With AI blamed for mass layoffs, here's how we can ensure workers get a fairer deal
science.summary: Is artificial intelligence (AI) finally coming for Australian jobs?

science.title: Illustrated guide shines a light on Australia's lanternfish
science.summary: These glow-in-the-dark, googly-eyed fishes perform the biggest daily migration of any animal on the planet and are among the most abundant and important fishes in our oceans. But they are also among the most mysterious. Now, Australian researchers finally have access to a comprehensive guide to aid in the identification of Australian lanternfishes.

science.title: Astronomers reveal the oceanic origin of Europa's sodium cloud
science.summary: Jupiter's moon Europa is a world of scientific intrigue, with a global ocean believed to lie beneath its icy crust. Now, observations from W. M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island, reveal something unexpected: the enormous, diffuse cloud of sodium surrounding Europa has remained remarkably stable across more than two decades of observations, despite the dynamic environment surrounding Jupiter.

science.title: Reef fish aren't so vulnerable to ocean acidification, after all
science.summary: In 2016, biologist Sandra A. Binning and a group of young researchers traveled to Australia's Lizard Island Research Station, at the northern end of the Great Barrier Reef in the Coral Sea.

science.title: Why nanoparticles struggle to reach ovarian cancer cells
science.summary: Microscopic particles called nanoparticles hold promise for delivering cancer treatments directly to tumors, potentially making therapies more effective while sparing healthy cells. But a major obstacle stands in the way: Other cells in the body can intercept these tiny particles before they reach their intended targets.

science.title: The networking paradox: Knowing more people can make you less trustworthy
science.summary: In the business world, knowing the right people is often considered a passport to success. A well-connected professional can introduce colleagues to new clients, bring together experts from different departments or create collaborations that would otherwise never happen. But there is a catch: The people best positioned to connect others may also be the ones others are least inclined to trust.

science.title: Study reveals hidden evolutionary diversity in endangered white pines
science.summary: Accurate species delimitation is fundamental to biodiversity conservation, yet it remains a persistent challenge in species-rich plant groups, particularly conifers, where convergent evolution, gene flow and incomplete lineage sorting often obscure species boundaries.

science.title: Dark energy may originate from known laws of particle physics
science.summary: For nearly three decades, scientists have struggled to explain one of the universe's most enduring mysteries: how a component known as dark energy is driving the accelerating expansion of the cosmos.

mix_items.title: Experimental anesthetic may also blunt pain at nonsedating doses
mix_items.summary: Common intravenous anesthetics such as propofol and etomidate usually require additional pain medicines. Propofol and etomidate enhance GABA-A receptors, which act as brakes on nerve-cell activity, but generally do not relieve pain at nonsedating doses. In addition, propofol is known to commonly cause low blood pressure and slowed (or sometimes stopped) breathing, while etomidate can cause adrenal suppression by lowering cortisol production, potentially causing severe or life-threatening effects. Therefore, researchers are looking for suitable alternatives.

mix_items.title: Deep Venture: A new class of ocean exploration vehicle developed
mix_items.summary: Researchers have a new capability for exploring some of the least understood regions of the ocean. Developed by Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) in collaboration with NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, Deep Venture is a next-generation autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) for deep-ocean research, capable of supporting a wide range of scientific missions, from shallow coastal waters to the deepest places on Earth. It can withstand extreme pressure, rated for depths of up to 11,000 meters (about 6.83 mi), or full ocean depth.

mix_items.title: Theory explains how fusion plasmas enter a state of improved energy confinement, solving a 40-year puzzle
mix_items.summary: Nuclear fusion promises a source of energy by combining light atomic nuclei, the same process that powers the sun. To achieve fusion on Earth, scientists must heat a gas to extreme temperatures, creating a charged state of matter called plasma. Keeping this plasma hot and stable long enough for fusion energy production is one of the main challenges facing the technology.

mix_items.title: More worried, yet more hopeful: The paradox of young people's climate action
mix_items.summary: New research from NIHR School of Public Health Research, published in the Lancet Planetary Health, provides new insights into how taking action on climate can impact young people's climate change distress, mental health and well-being.

mix_items.title: Killer whales became fearsome predators long before scientists thought
mix_items.summary: Killer whales, or orcas, are among the ocean's most formidable predators, hunting everything from fish and seals to other whales. But how and when these members of the dolphin family evolved into such effective hunters has long been something of a mystery.

mix_items.title: How desert biocrusts respond to changing snow cover
mix_items.summary: In the desert, winter snow may seem like a temporary visitor, but its effects can last long after the snow melts. By supplying water to dry ecosystems, snowfall helps sustain biological soil crusts (biocrusts), thin living layers on the soil surface that play important roles in desert ecosystems.

mix_items.title: Excitons mimic light in atom-thin material, confirming decade-old quantum prediction
mix_items.summary: Combining their skills in theory and experiment, Yale researchers have observed for the first time a type of energy-carrying composite particle move in a highly unexpected way. It's a finding that could lead to advances in quantum technologies, solar energy, LEDs and other optoelectronic technologies. The work is published in Nature Physics.

mix_items.title: Some allergies may start with cells running short of energy, not immune system misfires
mix_items.summary: Scientists are challenging centuries-old teaching that allergies start in the immune system, suggesting instead that they may be due to a power failure inside the body's barrier cells, which line the skin, gut, nose, lungs and esophagus.

mix_items.title: Could an erectile dysfunction drug offer a new way to treat Alzheimer's?
mix_items.summary: A drug developed to treat erectile dysfunction might seem an unlikely treatment for Alzheimer's disease. But researchers are increasingly interested in whether medicines such as Viagra could also help protect the brain.

mix_items.title: Resistance training could help boost brain health and confidence in older adults
mix_items.summary: Think about the last time you stood up from a chair or lifted a heavy shopping bag from the floor. These movements might feel automatic, but they take a surprising amount of coordination between your brain and your muscles.

mix_items.title: Genetic data from over one million people reveals new clues to how endometriosis develops
mix_items.summary: In a large, international study analyzing data from over 1 million people, researchers identified multiple genomic regions, associations and pathways underlying endometriosis, a debilitating, chronic condition in which tissue similar to the lining of the uterus grows in other places in the body.

mix_items.title: Researchers trace shifting pulsation modes in δ Scuti star KIC 4737720
mix_items.summary: Stars in the night sky may look calm and unchanging, but some are in fact constantly "vibrating." Just as a musical instrument can sound several notes at once, a star can pulse in several modes simultaneously. By measuring minute changes in a star's brightness, astronomers can read these stellar vibrations and, in turn, probe the physical processes at work inside it.

mix_items.title: Venus-like conditions reveal how minerals could preserve traces of ancient water
mix_items.summary: Venus is one of the most inhospitable environments in our solar system, with surface temperatures hot enough to melt lead and atmospheric pressure nearly 100 times greater than Earth's. Yet its surface may preserve clues to a time when the planet looked much more like Earth.

mix_items.title: Opioid misuse recognized, but not always recorded, national survey finds
mix_items.summary: Primary care clinicians who recognized opioid misuse in their patients did not always record it in the medical record, according to a national survey of 1,470 clinicians led by researchers at Wake Forest University School of Medicine.

mix_items.title: PTSD may shape the human brain differently depending on gender, race and the age at which a person's trauma occurred
mix_items.summary: Stress and trauma can leave molecular marks in the brain that may help explain the development of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). A study published in the journal Cell Reports on Nov. 20 that examined the postmortem brains of 101 people with PTSD found that genes associated with PTSD varied more than expected across different brain regions when it comes to DNA methylation, a natural biological process that acts like a genetic "dimmer switch" for genes, sometimes blocking genetic code entirely.

mix_items.title: Male bumblebees contribute to nest care, challenging view that they only mate
mix_items.summary: For decades, researchers have assumed male bumblebees' contribution to hives consisted mainly of DNA. However, a new study finds that the males actually help incubate baby bumbles, and that with males' assistance, hives thrive. The study, published in the Royal Society Open Science journal, quantifies the beneficial effects of having male babysitters in the hive.

mix_items.title: Low-viscosity lavas reveal a key to Mars's past
mix_items.summary: Since 2021, the Mars Perseverance rover has been roaming Jezero Crater, gathering details about the red planet's geology and hints about its past. On its journey, the rover took close-up images of the Séítah formation, a nearly 4-billion-year-old layer of rock at the base of the crater.

mix_items.title: Late-night phone use linked to shorter sleep in teens, especially girls
mix_items.summary: Checking the first notification after turning off the wake-up alarm, then endlessly scrolling through reels until sleepy. For many teenagers, the phone is never too far away. Excessive screen time has been linked to physical and mental health problems among teenagers, and its tentacles run deeper for the age group that is particularly vulnerable to body image issues. Scientists suspect the effects can extend beyond waking hours, reaching into an essential part of the body's daily routine: sleep.

mix_items.title: New liver model for studying alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency
mix_items.summary: AATD is a rare genetic metabolic disorder that affects the liver and lungs. A mutation causes liver cells (hepatocytes) to form misfolded alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT). This misfolding results in reduced secretion of AAT into the blood plasma. AAT plays an important role in controlling inflammatory processes in the body by mitigating excessive reactions that lead to tissue damage.

mix_items.title: Mobile streaming habits offer global societal insights
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the University of the Sunshine Coast observed how a total of 959 consumers in the U.S., South Korea and Germany used mobile streaming services.

mix_items.title: A star's last gasps: ALMA reveals a giant gas ring and budding hourglass around a star in transition
mix_items.summary: Stars like our sun don't die quietly. In their final act, they swell into red giants, shed their outer layers into space and leave behind a glowing, often strikingly sculpted cloud of gas called a planetary nebula. That transformation is thought to take only a few thousand years, a blink in the life of a star, so catching one in the act is rare.

mix_items.title: MYC inhibitor drug targets cancer cells directly and via the immune system
mix_items.summary: In a series of experiments, researchers have found that an experimental MYC inhibitor drug not only targets lung cancer cells directly but also makes cancer cells easier for the immune system to target and kill.

mix_items.title: We found a seaweed that hadn't been spotted in 90 years—and discovered vast underwater forests
mix_items.summary: A tangle of long, caramel-colored seaweed. That's what botanist A.H.S. Lucas found in 1935 while conducting research near Lord Howe Island, a World Heritage–listed site known for its unique biodiversity. After collecting some large adult specimens of this previously unidentified seaweed, Lucas named it Sargassum howeanum.

mix_items.title: High blood sugar powers an experimental implant that helps improve glucose control in diabetes
mix_items.summary: High blood sugar, a major problem in type 2 diabetes, could become part of the solution in monitoring the disease. Researchers have developed an experimental implant called NeuroAxis that utilizes a glucose fuel cell to harvest energy and sense metabolic fluctuations in real time.

mix_items.title: A protein in the brain's immune cells may accelerate damage in Alzheimer's disease
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Lund University in Sweden have identified a key role for the protein galectin-3 in Alzheimer's disease. The study shows that galectin-3 not only influences how the brain's immune cells, known as microglia, react to the disease's characteristic amyloid plaques but also shapes the plaques themselves—and may contribute to the nerve damage that develops around them.

mix_items.title: Malaria antibody protects infants but lowers immune response to R21 vaccine, trial finds
mix_items.summary: A single intramuscular dose of an experimental malaria monoclonal antibody safely provided infants with strong protection during Mali's six-month malaria season. However, potential interference with the R21 malaria vaccine is putting plans to pursue development of L9LS for this age group on hold, according to results from a clinical trial presented at the annual meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (ASTMH).

mix_items.title: New model predicts critical temperature of superconductors
mix_items.summary: Superconductivity, the ability to carry current with no resistance, has been found in materials ranging from metals to oxides. Conventional Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer (BCS) theory explains low-temperature metal superconductors well, but struggles with high-temperature oxide superconductors.

mix_items.title: Malaria vaccine shows 87% efficacy in clinical trial
mix_items.summary: The novel, genetically attenuated whole-parasite PfSPZ-LARC2 Vaccine for malaria achieved an 87% efficacy rate in preventing infection during a recent phase 1 trial.

mix_items.title: With AI blamed for mass layoffs, here's how we can ensure workers get a fairer deal
mix_items.summary: Is artificial intelligence (AI) finally coming for Australian jobs?

mix_items.title: Illustrated guide shines a light on Australia's lanternfish
mix_items.summary: These glow-in-the-dark, googly-eyed fishes perform the biggest daily migration of any animal on the planet and are among the most abundant and important fishes in our oceans. But they are also among the most mysterious. Now, Australian researchers finally have access to a comprehensive guide to aid in the identification of Australian lanternfishes.

mix_items.title: Gut stem cells go into overdrive with age—now scientists see a way to restrain their growth
mix_items.summary: A telltale sign of shortened life expectancy emerges in the gut with a hyperproliferation of stem cells, report scientists who have documented a dysregulation of these cells and defined them as a marker for aging across several species.

mix_items.title: Public code is not always reusable: Review uncovers gaps in medical study documentation
mix_items.summary: The data and code that underpin a research study can tell us what was actually done, and how. In a medical study, for example, how were patients selected for inclusion? How were missing values handled? How were the results evaluated? Access to a study's data and code helps researchers to answer these questions, to examine the methods and to build on the work.

mix_items.title: Astronomers reveal the oceanic origin of Europa's sodium cloud
mix_items.summary: Jupiter's moon Europa is a world of scientific intrigue, with a global ocean believed to lie beneath its icy crust. Now, observations from W. M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island, reveal something unexpected: the enormous, diffuse cloud of sodium surrounding Europa has remained remarkably stable across more than two decades of observations, despite the dynamic environment surrounding Jupiter.

mix_items.title: Reef fish aren't so vulnerable to ocean acidification, after all
mix_items.summary: In 2016, biologist Sandra A. Binning and a group of young researchers traveled to Australia's Lizard Island Research Station, at the northern end of the Great Barrier Reef in the Coral Sea.

mix_items.title: World-first study identifies genetic markers of young-onset type 2 diabetes in Chinese population
mix_items.summary: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK)'s Faculty of Medicine (CU Medicine) has conducted the world's first and largest genetic association study of age at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes in a Chinese population. The study identified three genetic regions associated with younger disease onset, impaired insulin-producing beta-cell function, and poorer blood glucose control.

mix_items.title: Why nanoparticles struggle to reach ovarian cancer cells
mix_items.summary: Microscopic particles called nanoparticles hold promise for delivering cancer treatments directly to tumors, potentially making therapies more effective while sparing healthy cells. But a major obstacle stands in the way: Other cells in the body can intercept these tiny particles before they reach their intended targets.

mix_items.title: The networking paradox: Knowing more people can make you less trustworthy
mix_items.summary: In the business world, knowing the right people is often considered a passport to success. A well-connected professional can introduce colleagues to new clients, bring together experts from different departments or create collaborations that would otherwise never happen. But there is a catch: The people best positioned to connect others may also be the ones others are least inclined to trust.

mix_items.title: National study highlights flexible approaches to integrating pharmacists in aged care
mix_items.summary: A national study led by researchers from RMIT University and the University of Canberra (UC) has identified practical strategies to support the integration of on-site pharmacists in residential elder care homes across metropolitan, regional, rural and remote Australia.

mix_items.title: Study reveals hidden evolutionary diversity in endangered white pines
mix_items.summary: Accurate species delimitation is fundamental to biodiversity conservation, yet it remains a persistent challenge in species-rich plant groups, particularly conifers, where convergent evolution, gene flow and incomplete lineage sorting often obscure species boundaries.

mix_items.title: Dark energy may originate from known laws of particle physics
mix_items.summary: For nearly three decades, scientists have struggled to explain one of the universe's most enduring mysteries: how a component known as dark energy is driving the accelerating expansion of the cosmos.

mix_items.title: Insecticide exposure in pregnancy linked to cognition in middle childhood
mix_items.summary: Neonicotinoids are among the most common insecticides worldwide, given their low cost and high efficacy. However, these insecticides take a long time to break down in the environment and can easily contaminate their surroundings, affecting food and water supplies. Despite the well-documented effects of neonicotinoids on insects and the environment, their impact on humans remains less clear.

mix_items.title: What is 'fascia release' and do I need to do it? A physical therapy expert unpacks the evidence
mix_items.summary: Are your hips constantly "tight"? Do you have bad posture? Are you stressed? According to the wellness world, it's probably your fascia (pronounced "FASH-ah"). This is the new buzzword explanation for many of your ailments: your fascia is tight, stuck, stiff or even dehydrated—and you need to "release" it.

mix_items.title: Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months
mix_items.summary: A new clinical trial found that the ketogenic diet dramatically outperformed Mediterranean and low-fat diets in reducing liver fat and improving metabolic health, even when participants lost similar amounts of weight. After just four to five months, about half of those following keto no longer met the criteria for prediabetes, while their liver fat dropped by an average of 67%.

mix_items.title: Molecular glues: Unlocking new targets in cancer
mix_items.summary: The human genome encodes several hundred E3 ligases—the enzymes that decide which proteins a cell destroys. Drug developers have so far harnessed a small number of them. In a new review in Molecular Cell, researchers at Karolinska Institutet and the University of Verona argue that the rest of these E3 ligases are where the next generation of cancer drugs will be found.

mix_items.title: Last Javan rhino habitat caught between mining plans and relocation debate
mix_items.summary: JAKARTA — Indonesian lawmakers and environmental groups are urging the government to revoke a mining map covering part of the waters around Ujung Kulon National Park, home to the world’s last surviving Javan rhinos. The calls were in response to a proposal by Hashim Djojohadikusumo, a mining and energy tycoon and the brother of President […]

mix_items.title: This simple habit is linked to a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's
mix_items.summary: Reading for pleasure may have surprisingly powerful benefits for the brain, with studies linking it to better memory, reduced stress, improved mental health, and a lower risk of dementia. Researchers highlight findings that just five minutes of fiction can reduce stress by up to 20%, while reading has also been associated with a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.

mix_items.title: Fossil fuels’ role in Africa’s energy transition contested as UN climate conference closes
mix_items.summary: As the 2026 edition of the annual U.N. Climate Change Conference reaches its conclusion in Antalya, Türkiye, on Nov. 20, African governments are arguing for increased financial and technical support to respond to climate change. Top priorities include more money for protection of forests and other landscapes, funding to help vulnerable communities and economies adapt […]

mix_items.title: Nickel linked to deforestation in Indonesia traded on London Metal Exchange, says report
mix_items.summary: Two companies approved for trading nickel on the London Metal Exchange (LME) could be linked to supply chains that have cleared primary rainforest in Indonesia, according to a report published by the NGO Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA). The NGO investigated two LME-approved Indonesian refiners – PT CNGR Ding Xing and PT Eternal Nickel Industry (ENI) […]

mix_items.title: A mysterious 4,000-year-old wall is rewriting North Africa’s history
mix_items.summary: A remarkable 4,000-year-old defensive structure discovered in Morocco is rewriting what scientists thought they knew about ancient North African civilizations. The massive fortifications reveal unexpectedly sophisticated prehistoric societies and suggest that the region played a much greater role in Mediterranean history than previously recognized.
